Of course the difficulty is to get reinforcements for the odd unit-that is to say, to get a man to come to some unit he does not know. That is always the difficulty with reinforcements. We have had much difficulty in the past, and with a proper effort we should not have a great deal of difficulty in the future in that regard. That is the situation with respect to recruiting.
So, do not let my hon. friend think that a recruiting campaign has been put on and that it has failed, because no such thing has happened at all. We shall tell the people of Canada what is to be done. We are going to put on the necessary campaign in order to inform them. We will ask, as a matter of fact, for citizens' committees in each province. We shall probably make allotments to each province, and ask that citizens' committees

British Columbia Telephone Company
be set up, and ask them to help get these men for the armed forces of Canada. I little doubt that the men will be provided. And when my hon. friend speaks of going by the back door instead of by the front door, I say to him that he might as well tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that he ought not to go by the back door and form loan committees throughout Canada to ask for loans, when he asks the people to lend their money to Canada. He might as well say that the Minister of Finance ought to go by the front door and put a compulsory levy on everybody in Canada, requiring each to subscribe a definite amount to its war loan, regardless of whether they want to or not.
There is no occasion for anybody to feel jittery with regard to the man-power situation. As I said the other day to the press, this matter ebbs and flows. We have been concerned vitally with material. We have been wondering where the material would come from. It is coming. I have been down in the east, in various training camps throughout the eastern part of the dominion, and I know it is coming. Now there is need to give attention to the question of men, not so much for units already formed, but for the formation of new and additional units, and for the keeping up of reinforcements. That is what is being done at the present time.
I want to ask this house and my hon. friend-I want to ask hon. members to give us help in connection with this matter. It is drab; it is unspectacular. It is not the same as passing a resolution, laying down a policy, or anything like that. But I would ask that hon. members give the necessary help from the point of view of indicating to the men that the time has come when they are needed. The fact is that they are needed in artillery, ordnance, and signal units perhaps considerably more than in infantry units.
Speaking of infantry, I am thinking of a unit, one which in fact my hon. friend must know. I found that that unit had about two hundred men under training as reinforcements in Canada. I am sure it has two hundred to two hundred and fifty men as reinforcements overseas. I was informed on the training ground that they had about two hundred more available in the depot. That is six hundred men for reinforcement of a unit which have not yet been required. So that there are cases where infantry units have surplus requirements. Artillery and other units took some of them, when they increased their establishments in addition to taking men who had been held as reinforcements for these particular units.
In order that we may help in that respect, in order that we may make no greater drain
on the man-power of Canada than was necessary, in order that industry might not be unduly disturbed I stated to the press the policy that as the men who are trained for four months leave their training they will be detailed to the units which are doing coastal defence duty in Canada, thereby enabling the men in the coastal defence units in Canada to go overseas, to join overseas units. In addition to that, if we. find it necessary, the men who have been enlisted for overseas service, and have been posted to one arm of the service, may probably be posted to some other arm where they are needed.
I feel it is part of the day's work of the Department of National Defence to get these men. It is part of the day's work to get these men in, have them realize their duty and realize the need. And I have little doubt that we will be successful, and that the number of men required will be obtained.

speechtext: Mr. G. G. McGEER (Vancouver-Burrard) moved the first reading of Bill No. 27 (from the senate) respecting the British Columbia Telephone Company.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY
speechtext:
This is a bill to amend the charter of the British Columbia Telephone company, which was granted in 1916. At thac time the company, having a dominion charter, brought together practically all the telephone operations of the province, with the exception of the Okanagan valley. At that time there were some 39,000 telephone services in the province. A capital of $10,000,000 was provided in the twenty-five year interval, the company having absorbed all available capital. The services which were temporarily delayed during the depression have now recovered and a demand is being created in the province for new services at the rate of about 5,000 to
6,000	a year. The cost of the installation of such services runs from $1,000,000 to $1,250,000 a year.
The situation is that if the company is to meet the demands for new services it must have the power to increase its existing capital.
229S

British Columbia Telephone Company
The bill provides that the company shall have the power to apply from time to time to the board of transport commissioners for the right to issue new capital. Under its present powers this board has the right to set the terms, the amount and the conditions under which such issue may be put forth, should it be authorized. The public institutions primarily connected with this service are the cities and municipalities of the province, particularly the city of Vancouver. The matter has been placed before the city council of Vancouver and before the union of municipalities of the province of British Columbia. With the stipulation that they will have the right to be heard when any application is made to the board of transport commissioners for an increase in the capital issued, no objection has been raised to the amendment proposed. The matter has come before the finance department and the department of taxation, and no objection has been raised in these quarters provided they are given the right to appear before the board.
I should like to make it clear that this amendment does not authorize an increase in the company's capital by another $10,000,000; it merely authorizes the company to make application from time to time to the board of transport commissioners as new capital issues are required to sustain the progress of its service.
There are some other minor changes to be made. The increase in the board of directors from nine to eleven is proportionate to the increase in the company's business. There is an amendment providing for the redemption of the preferred shares. The fact is that the preferred shares issued already by the company were issued in the terms of a contract which is redeemable. Technically the powers which the company enjoys under its present charter do not permit them to carry out the terms of that contract.
There is a provision to permit the company to enter certain realms of modern communication activities. The operations of this company in British Columbia are provincewide. They supply to the radio services the communications which exist for broadcasting between communities. In addition the company has kept abreast of the times and has supplied the Pacific coast of British Columbia with a radiotelephone service. This is used not only by the logging and tugboat industries, but in a great many other places where it is not possible to lay a telephone line.
I had understood the first reading of this bill would go through automatically and that an explanation could be given on its second reading. I was not prepared to-day to do

more than recall what memory I had of the matter. If there are any other questions to be asked I shall be glad to answer them.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave under standing order 31 to move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, to call the attention of the house and the government to the critical situation caused by the recent cessation of work in the steel industry which must very seriously affect our war effort.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order. May I say to my hon. friend that I have no desire to prevent a discussion at the appropriate time of the question which he has raised, but I think the present moment is most inappropriate. I feel strongly that with respect to every question of the character raised we should consider it in the light of the larger situation which exists at the present time. My hon. friend has made reference to the fact that some particular strike must affect our war effort. My understanding is that he refers to a strike which took place this morning. If I am correctly informed, at the present time the Department of Labour is engaged in an effort to mediate this particular dispute; to settle it, if possible, by conciliation. I fear the discussion of the question in parliament at this time might materially prejudice the efforts of the department to have the matter settled as speedily as possible by amicable means.
I feel equally that to bring a particular strike in the steel industry to the attention of parliament at this moment in the manner in which my hon. friend is doing it, namely, as a matter of extreme urgency, is to give to the dispute a significance in the eyes of the enemy which I do not think it ought to be permitted to assume. I do not believe it is in the public interest that the dispute should be discussed here at this time. There will be opportunities, upon going into supply or upon other occasions, when my hon. friend can take up the matter. I submit that having primary regard to our war effort it is not advisable to precipitate a debate in this house at this moment on this particular question, and that my hon. friend should not press his motion

Labour Conditions-Hamilton
as being of such urgency as to require the adjournment of the house to discuss what he has in mind.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
May I ask a question before the hon. member replies? The hon. gentleman was good enough to send me a copy of his motion, and in it I read these words:
... to call the attention of the house and the government to the critical situation caused by the recent cessation of work in the steel industry.
May I ask the hon. member if that is a statement of fact? If it is, I think he is entitled at least to have his motion heard and perhaps discussed. But one swallow does not make a summer. Is there just one strike? If so, I suggest that the statement made in the motion is not based on fact. I am asking for information.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the house that I would not raise this question did I not deem it to be of the most urgent public importance and meriting immediate discussion by the house. The matters herein concerned I have sought to draw to the attention of the government ever since the session began, both last summer and last fall. This is not a solitary instance. My hon. friends are referring to the situation in Hamilton. But there has been a strike in a steel industry in Montreal since last Wednesday, and the situation is likely to spread right across Canada. Wherever there is a steel industry the workers will be in sympathy with those who are now on strike. That is why I say it is a matter of urgent importance to the house. Parliament should have knowledge of the position which employers in this country are taking. If the government refuses to afford this opportunity for discussion, the responsibility must rest upon the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend is right and this condition has existed since last summer, I do not see how he can say it is urgent.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: I did not say that. I pointed out that the conditions leading to the present situation, that is the attitude of employers, had existed ever since this war began, and as a matter of fact for a long time before. But to-day we are facing a ruthless enemy; we are defending certain rights and privileges, certain freedoms and liberties. I cannot go to the workers of Canada while this present situation obtains and tell them that they have something worth while defending when they cannot open their mouths, cannot even attempt to organize to protect themselves without danger of dismissal.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Is the C.I.O. behind this?

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Whether it is the C.I.O. or the P.D.Q. does not matter. It is a lawful organization in the Dominion of Canada.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subtopic: STEEL INDUSTRY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT TO DISCUSS MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: If any other hon. member wishes to speak on this question, I shall be glad to hear him. If not, I must say that I am rather impressed by the statement made by the Prime Minister with regard to the seriousness of precipitating such a debate at this time. I have also heard in the course of the discussion that the situation which has arisen to-day is only one of a succession of such occurrences over some considerable time. The question I am now faced with, under the rules, is the question of the immediate public urgency of such a debate. In view of the opinions which have been expressed I am of the opinion that there is not that immediate public urgency which would necessitate this motion being debated now.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house adjourned on April 8, I was dealing with an amendment which I had just then moved on the subject of agriculture, and in particular on the condition of agriculture generally throughout the dominion. When it is realized that 35 per cent of the population of Canada are engaged in agriculture, I think it will be agreed that this nation cannot make its maximum -contribution to the war effort however prosperous the 65 per cent, the rest of the population, may be. Need I also say at the outset that no farmer worthy of the name Canadian has any desire at this time to profit at the expense of the empire as a whole. The farming population of Canada, however, believes that it is entitled to a fair return, a return sufficient to ensure a profit above cost of production. As has already been said on several occasions, for the twelve-year period, from 1926 to 1937, agriculture received only 11*3 per cent of the national income, and between 1930 and 1937 only 8-67 per cent of that income. It is interesting to note, with reference to the new policy, the quota system and summer-fallowing scheme, that under this policy western Canada will receive only $300,000,000. That figures out at 54 per cent of the income of the nation as a whole, which is estimated this year to amount to $5,900,000,000.
All that agriculture asks is that it shall receive the same consideration that other industries are receiving throughout the dominion. All it asks is that consideration which is given the manufacturing industries, as outlined by the acting Minister of Finance on October 12, 1939, as reported in Hansard of that date:
We must be able to hold out to business men the opportunity of making a reasonable profit

Supply-State oj Agriculture
and also the chances of securing some compensation for exceptional efficiency and willingness to take risks inherent in industrial enterprise in war time.
In those words the minister set forth what agriculture asks and what to date agriculture has been denied.
Again, the attitude of the British people so far as agriculture is concerned is indicated in an excerpt from a speech that was delivered early in 1940 by Sir Reginald Dorman-Smith, then Minister of Agriculture, who said:
Nobody nowadays wants to see extravagant or uncontrolled increases in prices such as occurred in the last war. We have learnt our lesson about that. All that the agricultural industry, as I know it, asks is precisely the same as any other industry requires, namely, that a level of prices should prevail which will enable the ordinary farmer under normal conditions to make a fair living for himself and to pay a fair and reasonable wage to his workers.
That quotation represents in my opinion a fair policy for agriculture whether in eastern or in western Canada, whether in the dairy, the live stock or the hog industry.
Something was said the other day with regard to prices of Canadian farm products as compared with those that prevailed in the last war. I secured from the bureau of statistics the prices of certain specified commodities during the years 1914, 1915 and 1916 and the same comparative prices for the years 1939, 1940 and 1941. In so far as wheat is concerned, in August, 1914, the cash price at Fort William was $1,081. In September, 1939, at the outbreak of war, the price was $0,739. Prices at other dates were as follows:

I intend to-day to speak not with regard to agriculture in general but with particular reference to the wheat problem. Naturally the first question that arises is, what has caused the increase in the production of wheat during the past few years? Why has the acreage in wheat been increased by some 3,000,000
acres since the beginning of the war? In my opinion the first and outstanding reason for this increase in acreage has been the lack of leadership of this government. That is evidenced by the fact that in November, 1939, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is reported to have stated that the grain exchange would remain open until wheat passed the price of $1.25. The only inference any farmer could take from that would be that in the opinion of the minister the price would increase.
Furthermore, speaking on December 13, 1939, the Minister of Agriculture made this statement:
We will have to get a good return out of our wheat to make up for that terrible trimming.
He was referring to the loss at that time.
Wheat, within the last two weeks, had risen above 80 cents a bushel and should go higher, he continued.
That was the attitude he took in December,
1939.	I realize that the Minister of Agriculture does not like any reference to some of the speeches he made during the election campaign, when according to the press reports he promised that there would be an interim payment of 10 or 12 cents a bushel. That he has denied, but he was so reported on a number of occasions. But among other things he allegedly said in March, 1940, in a speech delivered in the town of Earl Grey, Saskatchewan:
But the present government does not think it wise to sell all the Canadian wheat at 87 cents a bushel. The British government is not urging us to do so. If they bought it they would leave it right where it is in the elevators in Canada and pay the storage on it. . . .
We believe that Britain will pay us more for our wheat when she is ready to take it for consumption in England and that farmers would be well advised to allow the storage to be charged up to their participation certificates.
In other words the statement was that Britain was prepared to pay 87 cents a bushel.

speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What the Minister of Agriculture said to the western farmers was this: We could sell at 87 cents a bushel, but we think we can get you more. We believe that, as time goes on, the British government will pay more.
What has been the result? We do not know what the price is to-day that the British government is paying. We have endeavoured to get that information on several occasions. The premier of Saskatchewan apparently had the information, as did the minister of agriculture of the same province, when they stated in the legislature recently that 85 cents a bushel can be paid for the western farmers' wheat at Fort William because that is the price the British government is paying. Whatever the price is-and I cannot see any reason why we should not have that information- the fact remains that statements such as were made by the Minister of Agriculture during that campaign constituted an incentive for the western farmers to increase their wheat production. And if the British government was prepared to pay 87 cents a bushel, as was set forth on those two occasions, then this government stands indicted for paying storage on hundreds of millions of bushels since March, 1940, when the government of Britain was prepared to pay that price. These may have been only "guesstimates" but at least they were advanced as authoritative announcements and were relied upon by the western farmers.
I pass on. In November, 1940, the minister advanced another policy in which he set out in detail his viewpoint with regard to the wheat situation. I quote from Hansard of
November 14, 1940, at page 101:
On the supply side, Canada could expect to produce on an average 380 million bushels of wheat a year. That is her average for the last fourteen years and more than her average for the last five years, including the last two crops. Her total production in five years thus would amount to 1,900 million bushels. To this should be added the 280 million bushels carried over into 1940-41 from previous years, making a total quantity of 2,180 million bushels which it _ would be necessary for Canada to dispose of in the five year period.
It appeared, therefore, according to the above figures that Canada would have 2,180 million bushels of wheat to sell in the five year period, and that during the same period she probably would be able to market 2,080 million bushels, leaving a carryover at the end of that time of only 100 million bushels. Moreover, if Canada continued to be able to sell 30 million bushels a year to those countries outside Europe which were not being blockaded, instead of there being a surplus of 100 million bushels 
at the end of the five year period the demand for Canadian wheat would be 50 million bushels greater than the supply.
I ask the minister to tell this house what changes have taken place since November, 1940, that have made it necessary for him to alter the stand which he then took, that under his five-year plan at the end of that period there would be no wheat or very little wheat over.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not yet altered it.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister says he has not yet altered it. What he has done is he has placed before the country and before this house a new policy based upon a reduction in wheat acreage and a bonus for the growing of coarse grains. Invariably the answer he gives is that the surplus we have to-day is a war condition, that it has not resulted from any failure on the part of the government. Well, a reading of Hansard from 1930 to 1935 shows that at that time members of this government ridiculed the suggestion that wheat was unsalable. Their refrain, throughout western Canada at all events, was "Sell the wheat." What do the records show? Do they show that a greater proportion of wheat has been sold by the Canadian government since 1935 than was sold from 1930 to 1935? Our exports during 1930-35 were as follows:

speechtext:
Yes, but so did
the dry weather of 1931, 1932, 1933 and 1934. The government says the war is responsible for the carryover of some 550,000,000 bushels that exists to-day. In my opinion this excuse is

23U7
Supply-State oj Agriculture
not tenable except to the extent of our exports to Norway, Denmark, the low countries and France, which did not amount to more than 35-3 million bushels per annum at the time the war broke out. In support of what I state let me quote from the Monetary Times for January, 1941, at page 104. This is an article by E. Gurney Evans, of the Sanford Evans Statistical Service, who says:
The present Canadian wheat situation has not been caused by the war and will not be cleared up automatically by a victorious peace. Canada's exports in the first year of hostilities were actually higher than the average of the five years before the war. In fact our exports to enemy countries and those now occupied by him, all of which are blockaded by the British fleet, have been small in -recent years. Accurate estimates of Canada's exports of wheat by final countries of destination have been available only since 1936-37 but for the three-year period for which returns are available, only a yearly average of 35-3 million bushels went to the now blockaded group. The stopping of so comparatively small a flow cannot be blamed for our present excess supply.
I should like to read also from another authoritative source, an article by Mr. C. M. Short, appearing in Canadian Business of March, 1941, at page 59:
In fact, -the difficulties in which wheat growers now find themselves -and the serious attendant effects upon a national economy already strained to the utmost, are of earlier origin.
That is, earlier than the war.
In the past decade, the exportable supply of the surplus wheat countries averaged nearly 800 million bushels per annum as against average yearly imports of 630 millions by deficit countries, most of whom greatly, and in some cases entirely, lessened their dependence upon foreign wheat by increasing their own plantings, establishing uneconomic prices for domestic cereals, erecting high tariff walls and decreeing -stringent milling regulations to enforce the use of their own grains.
Elsewhere the article reads as follows:
The recent unfavourable developments affecting our wheat producers would not in themselves have caused the serious problems which have confronted Canada since .a near-record crop loomed up last summer. True, the European market was lost to overseas wheat exporters (of which Canada is the largest) when France, -the low countries and Scandinavia fell into the grip of naziism and the Mediterranean was closed to Italy. But continental Europe has not been an important market for Canadian wheat for several years, -the exports in that direction averaging less than 50 million bushels per annum since 1934.
So, having regard to what these authorities say, it would appear that the excuse that the war has caused this difficulty is untenable. It is true that the war decreased the world export of wheat, but it did not decrease Canada's peace-time share; and if war had not intervened there would have been a
.larger world trade in wheat but the United States, Argentina and Australia would have been supplying their share of the market.
What has been the attitude of this government since 1935? First there was the fire sale. Then they were going to find markets. Then we remember the promises made during the provincial election with regard to the price the farmers would receive. Then in November, 1940, the Minister of Agriculture enunciated his five-year prophecy, not a five-year policy. Then in March, 1941, the laissez-faire and drift which have characterized this government's wheat policy since 1935 were swept aside in one stroke, and regimentation and control were substituted. The government is practically the only market for wheat in Canada to-day. It owns all the wheat, and it will be in the wheat business at least until peace is restored and during the period of reconstruction. All the promises that were held out; all the statements made by the minister; all the rosy pictures of the prices that would be paid-all this is swept aside, and to-day in effect the farmer is placed undergovernment edict as to acreage and price. The farmer is to be paid for summer-fallowing, his land. There is to be a quota of some twelve bushels an acre. The present acreage is to be reduced by 35 per cent and the price is to be left at 70 cents a bushel. Is it any wonder there is unrest in western Canada?
Here is the picture: With the price at 70 cents a bushel, with increasing prices of commodities purchased by farmers, even had there been no reduction in acreage the standard of living of the western farmer would have been greatly decreased. I am not one who says that great changes must not come. I believe that tremendous changes will come. I do say, however, that before the farmers of Canada are placed under a system of regimentation, the Minister of Agriculture should be in a position to show from experience what the result thereof will be. I say that because this announced policy is a definite step toward regimentation. And regimentation, if it is to be brought into effect, should be based on something more than chance.
Because of fortuitous circumstances and uncertainties of the future no one knows how it is going to turn out. In so far as the wheat problem is concerned, the policy of drift and expediency of the last five years is now to have substituted a policy depending for its administration upon the will of the minister, not the certainty of a statute. No one knows what the policy means. No one knows when the regulations are going to be changed. One day shortly before the Easter adjournment the minister said the regulations had been

speechtext:
It would seem that we are now going to have a third set of regulations. The minister has said he is going to give parliament an opportunity to amend. Oh, no; the regulations will be brought before parliament so that he may have an excuse. Those regulations are not the regulations of parliament; rather they are those of the government of Canada. I have no doubt that the only reason why they were brought before the house was for the purpose of securing suggestions from hon. members. One of my main arguments against this provision is that $35,000,000 is to be expended under regulations. The farmers of western Canada have had one experience with regulations-and those regulations were based on a statute known as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Under that statute the farmers' rights were defined. The governor in council was specifically given power to pass regulations to give effect to the act, and under the regulations passed under that act many people in western Canada were deprived of the bonus, although entitled thereto under the statute.
Under its operation a vast army ot inspectors was created. In 1940, there were ninety-five appointees in Regina, and 188 in field service in Saskatchewan. Of that number 177 were inspectors and eleven supervisors. The vote of $35,000,000 now before us can be used for

Supply-State oj Agriculture
the same purpose. In the administration we may find that instead of the administration of law based upon statute, it may develop into the administration of lawlessness based upon the minister's own private interpretation, and interpretations of regulations made according to the whims of the minister's appointees.
If the minister had desired that benefits to the extent of $35,000,000 might flow to the Canadian farmers, how much easier it would have been for him to have fixed the total amount of crop the government would take at 230,000,000 bushels and given the farmer 85 cents a bushel, as was recommended by the legislature of Saskatchewan, an increase of 15 cents a bushel over the present price. Do hon. members know what that will amount to? Fifteen times 230,000,000 is equal to $34,455,000. If the farmer had been given a price of 85 cents a bushel, it would not have cost the people of Canada any more. But there would have been this drawback, as far as the minister is concerned. It would not have permitted the sum of $500,000 being used for administrative expenses throughout western Canada. Once more, to administer these regulations, a form of bureaucracy is set up whereby in the administration of this vote partisanship will play its part.
The minister does not contend that a price of 70 cents, Fort William is fair. I remember when he spoke in the house, I think in November, he said that with that price the farmer would not secure much, if any, above his costs of production. Why not in the midst of war grant our farmers a reasonable price on a quota basis of the amount which can be sold abroad or processed in Canada? I repeat that a price of 85 cents a bushel would not cost the people of Canada any more than the summer-fallow scheme. Every farmer should be allowed to seed as much land as he wishes to crop, and the government would purchase only so much as it could dispose of in the overseas or domestic markets.
I am sure that the minister, in his recent trip through western Canada, found that western farmers are aroused as never before. The western farmer cannot understand why this legislation has been introduced in the form in which it has, why a price of 70 cents a bushel has been set, a price below the cost of production. The introduction of the inadequate policy for agriculture is convincing evidence of one thing, that this government seems to be insulated against realities. The price is lower than that of last year because an increase has taken place in the prices of things which the farmer must buy. Compared with last year's price, the price this year is worth only about 64 cents a bushel.
In connection with the prices of things which the farmer has to buy and of the things which he has to sell, I secured the index numbers of wholesale prices of Canadian farm products, fully and chiefly manufactured goods and raw and partly manufactured goods, from 1933 to February, 1941. Who has been enriched since the outbreak of the war? Has it been the farmer? The hon. member for Qu'Appelle I believe has done more for the western farmer than any other member in this house. He pointed out in detail to the house recently the amounts which have been paid to the great storage corporations since the outbreak of this war. I ask the Minister of Agriculture-possibly the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) can give some information on this-to explain why something has not been done to reduce the cost of storage, in view of the tremendous amounts of grain now being stored. These rates were reduced slightly about a year or a year and a half ago. They

were equitable when little grain was in storage, but today the situation is quite different. Great amounts have been paid to these companies, and yet the solicitude of the government for them has been so great that an order in council has been passed recently whereby those storage companies which set up storage facilities in Fort William and Port Arthur are to be allowed to write off the cost of same at the rate of 50 per cent in 1942 and 50 per cent in 1943.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was dealing with the question of the elevator companies and the necessity for a reduction in their storage charges for wheat.
There is another phase I should like now to deal with, and that is a reduction in freight rates in order to permit of the selling of western wheat for feed purposes in the maritime provinces. At the present time the domestic carload rates on wheat from Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, to Halifax, Nova Scotia, is 64 cents per one hundred pounds, and to Saint John 62 cents per one hundred pounds, whereas the export carload rate from Saskatoon to Halifax and Saint John is 49i cents per one hundred pounds.
Recently I was in Nova Scotia and had occasion there to discuss this matter with a number of people, and without exception the stand they took was that it would be in the public interest if arrangements could be made to reduce the domestic carload rate to equal that of the export rate, thereby permitting the distribution of wheat for feed purposes in the maritime provinces, with a consequent reduction in the amount kept in storage in western Canada.
Up to the present I have dealt with the government's policy just in general. I now come to the recommendations which have been placed on Hansard before, but which I shall place on Hansard again in order to set out what the Canadian federation of agriculture asked for, and in the main this was approved by the legislature of Saskatchewan. The recommendations with regard to wheat were as follows:
1.	That while an adjustment programme in production might be found necessary in the future it was not advisable at this time to introduce compulsory restriction of acreage seeded to wheat.
2.	That for the coming crop year the dominion government should undertake to announce the

total amount which the wheat board would be willing to purchase from the 1941 crop, and that this volume should be based on the estimated amount which the wheat board might reasonably be expected to market during the 1941-42 crop year.
3.	That in view of the inevitable restriction of deliveries, and in order to maintain the income of the western farm home, the 1941 initial payment for wheat should be increased.
4.	That, until the price of wheat reached and was maintained at a level commensurate with the price of things that enter into the cost of production, a processing tax of not less than 50 cents per bushel should be placed on all wheat milled for domestic consumption.
5.	That the carryover of grain at the end of the present crop year should be regarded as a wartime reserve to ensure the constant supply of wheat to Great Britain in the event of possible crop failure in the coarse of the war.
6.	That since the maintenance of reserve stocks of grain on the farm provides an effective form of crop insurance under existing conditions, the federal government should be asked to provide financial assistance to farmers for the construction of adequate farm storage facilities to enable the farmer to adjust his. deliveries in accordance with the conditions likely to exist during the 1941 crop period.
7.	That the payment of farm storage should be continued.
8.	That, since very (little storage space was likely to be available at the time of the 1941 harvest, the dominion government should authorize the wheat board to make cash advances against that portion of the 1941 crop which the farmer might be able to deliver under the plan outlined above.
That plan and those recommendations were supported by the legislature of Saskatchewan. Yet what do we find? In spite of the fact that the minister of agriculture and the premier of Saskatchewan supported these recommendations, as did every member of the legislature, the government of Canada introduces a policy which, as was so courageously pointed out by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), bears no resemblance to the suggestions or recommendations either of the representatives of agriculture or of the western farmer other than the acceptance of the reduction in the amount of wheat which the government will purchase during the year
1941	to the amount that will be marketed at home or abroad during this year.
The policy announced by the government is at best a one-year policy. It has no continuity. It begins and ends this year, and in
1942	the result will be that with normal climatic conditions a very much larger crop-of wheat will be harvested than has been produced in any year up to the present-that is, providing the farmers take advantage of the summer-fallowing provision. What is more-and this has not been mentioned-there will be a reduction in the revenue of the
AjPRIL 28, 1941
Supply-State of Agriculture
railroads by some $30,000,000, representing the freight rates between western Canada and Fort William on the amount of wheat over and above the 230 million bushels which will be purchased this year. That loss will have to be made up in some way, and as yet we have had no suggestion how it is going to be done.
This policy of the government pleases no one. It does not please the western farmer and it does not please the eastern farmer. Why was the policy enunciated by the Canadian federation of agriculture not accepted by the government? It would not have cost the people of Canada any more than the present policy and would have been acceptable to agriculture throughout the dominion as a whole.
On April 14, the Minister of Agriculture spoke on the radio in Saskatchewan, and among other things he said this:
"There is no use sugaring the pill by trying to convince you we are trying to do something for you," Mr. Gardiner told his farmer audience. "We are trying to do something for Canada and Britain and for the democratic way of living. It is not my intention to try to convince you that what we are asking you to do will help you financially."
That is an excuse, Mr. Speaker, and nothing but an excuse. Giving the farmer 85 cents a bushel for the wheat that can be disposed of by the Canadian government this year together with the amount processed in Canada would cost a matter of only $34,500,000. The present scheme will cost at least $35,000,000 and will run up to $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 depending upon the amount of land that is summer-fallowed. It is merely an excuse, an attempt to quiet the western farmer at this time, when he is just as anxious as any other person in Canada to contribute his bit in winning the war. One year of this policy in my opinion will spell ruination for western agriculture. It may mean the same for the eastern dairy farmer, the hog producer and the cattle raiser.
Last November the Minister of Agriculture made a prophecy, which was nothing but wishful thinking. His recent announcement means that he now indulges in wishful tinkering with the farm economies of both western and eastern Canada, with results that are uncertain to both. If the acreage in wheat in western Canada is reduced and the price for the crop which the farmer is allowed to raise is not increased sufficiently to cover the cost of production and bring about a parity with the costs of the commodities the farmer has to buy, western agriculture will be ruined. I represent a rural constituency, Mr. Speaker,
and I plead with the government to assure the farmers of Canada of a price that will be consistent with the cost of the things he buys.
This summer-fallow policy will please no one east or west, and I warn the minister that unless agriculture in this dominion is assured of a fair return, the morale of those engaged therein will be lowered, with a consequent lowering of our war effort.
In conclusion, I would ask a certain question: Has the British government requested Canada to reduce her food supplies? Has the British government asked Canada to reduce the production of wheat, or has Canada been asked to pile up tremendous food supplies for the day that will come, the day of victory, as portrayed in the words of the Prime Minister of Great Britain when he said:
We shall do our best to encourage the building up of reserves of food all over the world so that there will always be held before the eyes of the people of Europe, including-and I say it deliberately-the German and Austrian people, the certainty that the shattering of nazi power will bring to them all immediate food, freedom and peace.
I reiterate those words in the order in which they were given-food, freedom and peace. Mr. Churchill weighs his words carefully, and it is not without significance that food is the first named.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In putting his amendment before the house, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) used the words that had previously been used by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn). After the hon. member for Haldimand had spoken, this editorial appeared in the Toronto Globe and. Mail of March 28:
Mr. Mark Senn, the Conservative member for Haldimand, initiated a debate in the House of Commons upon the plight of the farmers, ancl, after a reasoned statement of the difficulty which surrounds the agricultural industry, called upon the government to take remedial measures.
Undoubtedly there are scores of members on the government side of the house who feel just as strongly about the matter as Mr. Senn. Most of them represent farming districts and have first-hand knowledge of the troubles which beset the primary producers. They could have told parliament what is wrong with rural Canada. They could have given information which would be invaluable to the Minister of Agriculture in any effort to grapple with the problem. What happened? According to our Ottawa correspondent, "the government feared its own farm supporters might join in the attack," and Hon. James G. Gardiner rose to reply. Our parilamentary reporter adds: "He at once placed the issue as a vote of confidence in the government, and assured the waverers on his own side that there would be plenty of opportunity to discuss the wheat policy and other farm policies once this amendment
Supply-State of Agriculture

(demanding price parity) was defeated. He charged that the amendment obstructed free discussion, free give-and-take on the merits of the government's policy."
All of which is pure eyewash. Surely it is possible for parliament to discuss the problems of the farmers without playing politics. What is parliament for if it is not to consider such matters?
It is quite possible that the editor and the reporter of the Toronto Globe and Mail were unaware of the rules of the house, but the hon. member for Haldimand was no doubt well aware when he made 'his motion that he was making this a party issue. He was well aware that he was proposing to put the farmer members on the spot by having them either support the government on a want of confidence motion or support his amendment. The hon. member for Haldimand, experienced parliamentarian that he is, knew that, when he moved his amendment to the government's motion that the house resolve itself into committee of supply, he was putting the debate upon a purely party basis. In my opinion, it is a pity that the hon. member should have put as important a question as this upon such a basis, because there is no one in this house who is prepared to argue that the farmers of Ontario, or for that matter the farmers of Canada, are making too much money or even enough. We are prepared to admit that. I am an Ontario farmer, and in my opinion the majority of the farmers have to struggle along in order to maintain a normal standard of living, to raise and educate their families and to pay their debts. But Canadian farmers are not the only class of people in this country who have to struggle to make a living. The same may be said of farmers in any country. You will find people struggling in the cities, wherever you go. My experience around the city is that city people could give farmers lessons on how to economize and pinch pennies. You will find a great deal more poverty, distressing poverty, in cities than among the farmers. We do not blame people for struggling and endeavouring to raise their standard of living; anyone who is ambitious will do that, no matter what his occupation may be. But in spite of the struggle, I believe that the bulk of our citizens normally are fairly happy.
There is no class of people making a great deal of money nowadays during this war. We hear a good deal of argument that farm prices ought to be put on a parity with the returns to labour and industry. A party of members was invited to visit the Canada Steel Company of Hamilton as its guests, and one of the things that I learned which I thought was quite interesting was that last

year while the output of that particular plant which we visited was up 50 per cent, their net profit was down 10 per cent. That indicates to me that the industries are not making a lot of money during this war.
Hotel keepers are supposed to be making plenty of money these days, but the owner of one of our best hotels in Pembroke, when in my office one day-he was in Ottawa looking after his income tax-gave me to understand that in spite of the fact that Pembroke is quite close to the military camp at Peta-wawa, so that, as I suppose, the hotel business there might be four or five times what it would be normally, as far as the beverage room is concerned, the net profit in that establishment will not be any greater than it was prior to the war. When you take 75 per cent of the excess profit from industry, from hotel keepers or from any one else who is making an excess profit, there is no one who will make much more than a living if we continue as we are doing under the present control of prices.
While I was listening to the hon. member for Haldimand in his contention that farmers were in dire distress, I was wondering whether he was thinking more of his own political future or of the political future of his party, or whether he was really sincere. When we as leaders in our ridings go among our people we try to convince them that the winning of the war is the only thing that matters for the time being, that that is the all important consideration. We must bend every effort to the destruction of this awful demon that is attacking the world to-day. But as I go throughout my riding I feel that I have a great deal of reason to be thankful for the spirit of the people of Renfrew North. I do not suppose Renfrew North is very much different from any other riding in Ontario, but my experience in travelling in that riding is that people of all classes and in all walks of life there are ready to sacrifice, to give and to work on behalf of the war effort. We find that spirit among all classes of men; business men, bank managers, leaders in industry, office managers; when any work in connection with the war effort is brought to their attention they are ready to give of their time and their money, to spend days and nights freely in working on behalf of the war effort. That is also true of women all through the riding and I suppose, all across Canada; our women are just as willing to give their time and labour.
I was pleased that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) expressed in this house his thanks to the volunteers who helped in the national registration. In my riding we

Supply-State of Agriculture
had hundreds of volunteers who were ready to use their cars to bring people in to register and who gave their time freely. In the town of Pembroke we have the Standard-Observer. It started a campaign on behalf of the British war victims' fund. The response was generous; no person canvassed any one, you simply went in with your dollar or your ten dollars or, in some instances, fifty dollars, and by that effort thousands of dollars were raised in Pembroke and the surrounding community for that fund. When the campaign was put on for the war savings certificates, the business men of the town got together, formed an organization and went to work, and almost one hundred per cent of the employees in Pembroke are having the deduction made from their pay cheques for the buying of war savings certificates. When we had our war charities drive, the men who had gone around last fall canvassing for the Red Cross did not complain because they were asked to do this; they spent days travelling on behalf of the war charities drive. When the salvage campaign was put on, we did not hear any grumbling about it; committees were organized, buildings arranged for, where the salvage could be accumulated and sorted and disposed of. In connection with the Red Cross work I had a letter from a farmer's wife in my riding. I heard a report of the amount this particular lady had done, and to assure myself that it was true I wrote to her and received in reply this letter dated March 13, 1941:
Dear Sir,-
It was a surprise to me when I received your letter to-day and where you would hear that is a mystery. Yes, I have finished 565 articles of Red Cross since we organized. I work at different articles and then you never tire: pyjamas, socks, hospital gowns, scarves, knee caps, wristlets, pneumonia jackets, quilt, hot-water B. covers, ice-bag covers, hospital socks, Hampton pads, sling bandages, abdominal binders, T. binders, personal property bags, etc. I sent my name in a pair of socks and got a very nice letter from an officer in England (Mr. Rae Gregson) so our work is appreciated, he said he came from a warm climate and when he landed there he felt the need of the nice articles that were in store for him.
And here is a sentence that I should like to record:
I just feel how little I am doing when I consider some poor mothers who have been brave enough to let 2, 3 and some four sons enlist.
I quote this just as an indication of the spirit of the people, not only in the towns but in the rural parts of my riding. This woman is an average farmer's wife, does her own work, does not hesitate about working outside as well as indoors. That spirit is very common as far as Red Cross work is
concerned. That remark about some mothers giving two or three or four sons reminds me of a doctor we have in the village of Eganville, Doctor Reeve. He has reached the three score years and ten; he has four sons, two of whom are overseas, one being in the air force in Canada and the other an interne in the Civic hospital, who expects to get into the army by the first of July. That exemplifies the spirit of our people. That spirit is a very precious thing, something we ought to safeguard and encourage. Any word or act that would have a tendency to discourage that spirit on the part of our people is, I believe, traitorous to the British empire.
It is the easiest thing in the world to create a spirit of self-pity in any class. You can create it among farmers or labouring men, and it is one of the worst diseases with which any individual or class could be afflicted. Cancer is bad, but I believe that self-pity is responsible for more unhappiness and discontent than ever could be the case with cancer. There are plenty of speeches made throughout the country that might have a tendency to create discontent among certain classes of people. That is bad enough, and it is dangerous; but when members of this house, leaders of the people, make speeches which have a tendency to create unrest and discontent, I believe that is much worse.

Oh, oh.

speechtext:
I do not think hon. members need to say "oh, oh." If they will read the speech they will see what I mean; it had the tone and all the other earmarks. I think we have been exceedingly fortunate in Canada in that we have had so little labour trouble; but if anything would have a tendency to create trouble and stir up discontent between labour and industry, it would be just speeches of that kind, both outside and inside this house, made by men elected to represent the Canadian people.
Then we had the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) making a speech that naturally would be expected to create unrest and discontent among our soldiers. I read the following quotation from that speech, as it appears in Hansard for March 11, 1941:
The minister must know that there is the greatest feeling of unrest among the men at this camp.
The hon. member was referring to the camp at Petawawa. Of course there is unrest among the working men and the soldiers, and they grumble, as is their privilege. Occasionally this sort of thing leads to trouble; and apparently, according to what was said to-day by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), his words have had some effect.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the inactivity of the government that has had an effect.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Naturally there would be some discontent at Petawawa, but when a member of parliament rises in his place and talks about that discontent, he simply encourages something which the soldiers themselves do not take at all seriously.
We have had more or less of a campaign to create discontent among the farmers right across Canada. There is a definite form of dicontent being fostered from both within and without this house, and that certainly is not good for our war effort. The hon. member for Haldimand did his best to foster that spirit of discontent. I was wondering whether he was really sincere, whether he was actually working on behalf of the farmers and was so greatly interested in their welfare, and I took the trouble to go back over the record of the last few years. I find that in 1929, when the Liberals were in office, the hon. member for Haldimand made a speech that was very similar to the one he made just a short time ago.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then he has been right for a long time.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I may have something to say about that later on. In 1929 the hon. gentleman said:
... let me say that ever since this government came into office in 1921, there has been a steady depreciation in land values. In many communities, large numbers of farm holdings are being offered for sale, and in many instances it is impossible to sell those farm holdings for the value of the buildings themselves. In fact, from my own observation and experience I feel that I am safe in saying that land values have depreciated by from thirty to forty per cent during the past seven or eight years, since this government came into power.
I quote now from the speech delivered by the same hon. member in 1941:
The great difficulty which surrounds agriculture to-day can be sized up, I think, in one sentence. It is this, that the income or the revenue of the average farm in Canada is not sufficient to-day to provide for costs of production and at the same time to maintain a reasonable standard of living for the farmer and his family. During the past twenty-five years a great change has come over agriculture throughout the dominion. In the years just prior to the great war and all through the great war, farmers of Canada enjoyed a modicum of prosperity, which has completely vanished at the present time.
And listen to this:
During the years which have followed that time they have found that their reserves have been largely dissipated, and land values in this country have dropped perhaps fifty per cent or more.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member deny the truth of those statements?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am principally interested in showing the hon. member just what happened in the intervening period. In 1929 the Conservatives were in office, and the hon. member for Haldimand supported that party.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; in 1929 the Liberals were in office.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Unfortunately.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am proud of that. But in 1930, after a vigorous campaign, the hon. member for Haldimand and his friends were able to convince the farmers that they were in such dire distress that it would be to their own advantage to return the Conservatives to power, and thereby assure themselves a higher standard of living. The farmers fell for that and elected the hon. member for Haldimand and his associates, who were put in the seat of government. But what happened? Prices immediately started to decline. It is interesting to note just how the hon. member for Haldimand reacted during the terrible years between 1930 and 1935. Was he on his feet telling of the hardships

Supply-Stale of Agriculture
of the farmers and urging the government to bonus this, put a premium on that, take the taxpayers' money to assist the farmers and so on, or what did he do?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us see the record.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry I have not anything greatly to the credit of the hon. member for Haldimand. I find that on November 24, 1932, the hon. member voted against an amendment to provide an opportunity for discussion of the deplorable condition of agriculture, and the refusal by the government to announce a policjr for agriculture.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did he do to-day?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then on March 15, 1932, the hon. member voted against a motion to reduce to 7 per cent the interest on bank loans. Does that record sound as if the hon. member were sincere when he introduced the amendment, or would it appear that he is thinking only of his own political future, and that of his party?
Let us look at some of the figures. I have before me prices of farm products on June 3, 1929, July 16, 1932, and March 5, 1941. Those
