In view of these figures I cannot believe that the hon. member for Haldimand was thinking only of Canada's war effort when he pictured the dire distress of agriculture under present conditions. Nor can I believe that the hon. member for Vancouver East was thinking only of the welfare of the British empire and its war effort when he made the speech from which a quotation was made a few moments ago.
Farmers in some communities have been able to help themselves in some ways. The tobacco growers in Norfolk county have banded together and have been able through their own organization to do a good deal toward stabilizing their market and controlling their prices. But they did it by controlling production. The whole-milk producers with the aid of legislation have been able fairly well to control the price of whole milk, and to stabilize that market. In making these observations I refer only to Ontario, under the regulations now in effect.
Only recently I read in a local paper an article which seemed to show how farmers in some communities were able to help themselves. This was a report from Spencerville dairy. I have found in reading the report that last year the net price per one hundred pounds of milk was $1.41. That looks high, and I believe that in that cooperative dairy group they pool their milk, and supply it to the village. Milk used in the manufacture of cheese netted them $1.08, but, as I have pointed out, their average per one hundred pounds for the season was $1.41.
This afternoon and for some days prior to the Easter recess we heard speeches respecting the government's policy in connection with western wheat. I believe it is too bad the government has found it necessary to get into the wheat business. An hon. member who spoke this afternoon deplored the regimentation of agriculture. I do not believe the farmers of Canada are particularly favourable to regimentation; but for some years the government has been drifting into the wheat business, and has certainly derived many headaches from its efforts.
There has been considerable criticism respecting the government's policy whereby it provides an acreage bonus for western
Supply-State oj Agriculture

farmers. We are in the business, and we must remember that in this war we have not France to which we can sell wheat. During the last war we sold wheat to that country as well as to Italy, but those countries are not getting our wheat now.
We have the wheat on our hands. The Minister of Agriculture attempted to keep the wheat acreage of Canada at its then level. He advised the farmers of western Canada not to increase their wheat acreage, but they went ahead and sowed some three or four million additional acres. What is going to be done with it? If we are going to set a price, then we must have some control over production. This is the first time that any effort has been made to control the production of western wheat. If we are in the wheat business, we must find some way of controlling production until we have the necessary markets.
The Minister of Agriculture has come in for considerable criticism, not only with respect to wheat but with respect to butter, cheese and bacon. Fortunately the minister developed a thick skin during his many years of public life, and I do not think he takes harsh criticism too seriously. That is fortunate, not only for the minister but for the people of Canada. If abuse and criticism got under the minister's hide, it would be just too bad. As we know him, he is always on top of his job and able to do his work. As I have observed him since I came into this house, I doubt if we could get a man anywhere in Canada as well equipped to handle the Department of Agriculture.
My attitude with regard to the government's effort to maintain the cause of agriculture is that the Minister of Agriculture knows agriculture from coast to coast as perhaps no other man in Canada. It is natural for the Ontario farmer to view these matters from the Ontario angle, and for the Saskatchewan farmer to view them from the Saskatchewan angle. But there are many different and difficult angles to this problem of agriculture and we should take the broad view of the matter. When the apple growers of British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Ontario got into trouble, the Minister of Agriculture was able to solve their difficulties. The same thing was true when we were faced with a surplus of butter. He did not handle that situation by fixing the price of butter; he handled it by putting a premium on cheese and encouraging the farmers to send their milk to the cheese factories.
I believe that we as farmers and as members of parliament ought to encourage the spirit of activity and the anxiety to help with our war effort which are abroad throughout

the country to-day. I do not think our farmers are doing so much worrying. They are anxious that we should put forth every effort to win the war. I think this spirit was very well exemplified by the convention of mayors which met here in Ottawa. They had a message for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), but because of the terrible war situation which had developed recently they decided just to pay him a friendly call and not to bother him with municipal matters. One of the greatest contributions which we can make as members is to encourage a spirit of cheerfulness and content among all classes of our people, among our labourers, among our soldiers and among our farmers.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to endeavour to follow the arguments just presented by the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren). It is hardly becoming to any member of this house to call into question the sincerity of either the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn), or the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). It ill becomes an hon. member to question the sincerity of another member. I imagine the hon. member who has just taken his seat is like the rest of us. If he shovels the snow off his own doorstep, he will not have much time for the hoar frost on other people's.
Discontent is not brought about by criticism; discontent is brought about by the failure of a governing body to keep pace with social needs. Apparently the hon. member for Renfrew North is not in harmony with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who made the statement a few weeks ago that the need of this parliament was a stronger opposition. Apparently the hon. member thinks that what we need at this time is an opposition which will believe that everything is lovely, that everybody is hopeful, that everyone is happy. That is not the task of an opposition. The task of an opposition is to present the facts as they find them in various parts of the country and bring them to the attention of the government. If the hon. member for Renfrew North will take the trouble to go through Hansard from 1930 to 1935 and read some of the speeches made by the present Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), or look up some of the speeches made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he was leader of the opposition in Saskatchewan, he will find that both of those gentlemen carried out their duties with remarkable ability.
Apparently the hon. gentleman who just sat down seems to think that the best way to get rid of discontent is to pretend that it is

Supply-Stale of Agriculture
not there. He reminds me very much of Louis XVI. When there were brought to him reports of disturbed social conditions throughout the France of that day, he kept saying, "After me, the deluge." But the deluge came in his time, and we all remember that Louis lost his head. Not that he had ever made much use of it when he had it, but he was never the same after he lost it.
Some of my colleagues will deal with the more general aspects of the plight of agriculture, so I shall confine myself more particularly to the growing and marketing of wheat. I do not wish to traverse the territory I covered the other evening, and I propose to be unusually brief.
The whole manner in which this wheat legislation and the government's wheat policy has been presented this session has been far from satisfactory. When we met here last November, questions were put to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) asking when we might have an opportunity of discussing the government s policy for marketing the 1941 wheat crop. The reply, it will be remembered, was that we would have an opportunity some time in February, when the government proposed to bring down its policy. When we met in February the question was raised again, but the matter was postponed week by week until at last the government's policy was brought down in a joint statement, one delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and one by the Minister of Agriculture on March 12. Here we are now at April 28, and no actual wheat legislation is before the house. The exact nature of the government's _ policy with Tespect to the delivery and marketing of wheat is still a matter of conjecture, and we know nothing at all about the regulations that are to be submitted by the wheat board.
The government's wheat policy as it has been presented is drawn up in two parts. One part is that which has to do with the marketing regulations. It proposes to reduce the amount of wheat which the farmers can deliver to 230 million bushels. That is the part of the policy which I would call the medicine. It is that part of the policy which the Minister of Agriculture himself told the house was going to cost the prairie farmer $100,000,000 this year. The other part of the policy is a very small dose of sugar intended to make the medicine palatable-a vote of $35,000,000, about $30,000,000 of which will, it is anticipated, go into the acreage reduction bonus.
The position of members of the house is' this, that we have the power to refuse or accept the sugar, but we must take the medicine whether we like it or not. We are presented with an estimate which we can vote for or reject. But no legislation has been
brought down with respect to the delivery and marketing of the wheat itself. In other words, the only thing which the government has brought down is something which the members cannot vote against because it is the compensation for the unpleasant part of the policy. The result is that the members of this house have had no opportunity whatsoever of recording either their approval or disapproval of the government's wheat policy.
The interesting thing to me is that not a single organization interested in agriculture and not a single member of the house, either government or opposition, apart from the Minister of Agriculture himself, have given to the government's wheat policy their unqualified approval. Members supporting the government one after another have registered their disapproval with one aspect or another of the policy. The member who got the closest to supporting it was the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). That hon. gentleman was kind enough to say in his remarks, after he had listened to me talking about wheat, that he thought I ought to go back and take care of my flock. I can say this at all events, that when I had finished my remarks, poor as they may have been, the house at least knew where I stood on the matter; but after listening to the hon. member for Moose Jaw for forty minutes, neither I nor any other member knew where he stood. In closing his remarks he said: "This policy may be good, and it may be bad, but only time can tell."

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And he was going to raise wheat anyway.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. Every other member who has spoken on the government side has condemned this policy. Every organization interested in agriculture whether in the east or in the west has spoken against this policy. Although the Minister of Agriculture took the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) to task on April 8, the hon. member was correct when he said that the essential part of the recommendations made by the Canadian federation of agriculture to the government had been left out of the government's policy. The bitter part the government accepted. The medicine has been doled out. But the sugar coating has been reduced and diluted until I am afraid it will not make the medicine very palatable.
A few weeks ago I suggested, on behalf of the group with which I am associated, six proposals. I shall not go over them except to summarize and in order to carry out the sequence of what I have to say.
We proposed that the initial minimum price ought to be higher. It will be remembered that two years ago Professor Allen of Sas-
Supply-State oj Agriculture

katchewan university said that the farmers needed 90 cents a bushel at their shipping point, which means $1.10 basis Fort William in order to produce wheat and make a living. If that was true in 1939, how much more true it will be next spring when most of the 1941 crop is going to be delivered. We pointed out and we still maintain that if the government insists on paying only 70 cents a bushel basis Fort William and allows the farmer to deliver only what will amount to 48 per cent of the wheat he delivered last year, the wheat industry is going to receive a tremendous blow.
The second thing we proposed was that there ought to be a maximum delivery of 1,000 bushels of wheat for each farmer. The man who is going to be hardest hit by the government's wheat policy is the small farmer. I talked during the Easter recess to farmers who had 2,000 acres in wheat last year. These men can adjust themselves to meet the government's policy to some extent. At least they can, I think, get by.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I talked to one farmer who had 2,000 acres in wheat last year, and he said, "I put practically every acre I had in wheat last year, and this year I propose to summer-fallow 600 acres." If we allow him twelve bushels to the acre on 65 per cent of last year's acreage, he will be able to sell quite a large amount of wheat. He has storage for seven or eight thousand bushels on his farm.
But take a man in the drought area. These farmers, as the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) knows very well, have been compelled very often to reduce their cultivated acreage and reduce drastically their wheat acreage. Some of them have reduced it to forty or fifty acres. What are they going to be allowed to deliver, and what benefit is the wheat acreage reduction bonus going to be to them? If they took their entire wheat acreage last year or the year before out of wheat, the amount of bonus they would receive would be negligible. That is why we ask for a maximum delivery to take care of the small farmer, particularly the small farmer in the drought area who has been compelled by lack of seed and unfavourable moisture conditions to reduce his wheat acreage over the past five or eight years.
Next we think the government should encourage the farmers to provide storage on their farms and make an advance for that purpose. Talking with farmers in the last two weeks, I find that many, especially those in the drought areas, have not recovered from the terrible conditions through which they have passed in

the last eight or ten years. They have not forgotten that in 1937 this government had to ship in $18,000,000 worth of seed. They have not forgotten that they had to sacrifice some of their best milk herds, that they had to send their horses down to the Carberry pasture, and that many of them were stacking Russian thistle and feeding it to their stock. They would feel more secure and the country would feel more secure if it were possible to store
200.000.	000 bushels on the farms of the prairies.
The fourth thing we asked was that there
should be a cash advance of 75 per cent of the initial payment. In replying to this the other day, the Minister of Agriculture said that it had been recommended last year and urged by several bodies, but the government had not done it and everyone seemed to be satisfied. I think the minister is partly correct when he says that the storage was found more rapidly than most people had thought possible and so the farmers were able to deliver their quotas. The minister is not suggesting, however, that the same will be true this fall. The Minister of Trade and Commerce gave figures the other day indicating that at the very best we shall have-
37.000.	000 bushels of storage space next fall, and it is to be taken for granted that the greater part of the 1941 wheat crop will have to be delivered next spring and that only a small part of it can be delivered in this calendar year. The argument that last year it did not prove to be necessary will not be valid this year, because this year we cannot expect the expansion of storage space by the building of annexes and that sort of thing which we had last fall. The government would be well advised to reconsider making a cash advance of some percentage of the-amount of money the farmer will get for the quota he will be allowed to deliver.
Our fifth proposal was the payment of storage charges on that wheat which the farmer grows over and above his quota, because we might as well reconcile ourselves to the fact that many farmers will say exactly what the hon. member for Moose Jaw says, "I will sow all my wheat as usual." Many farmers will not; but there are many who will, and we should remember that there are large areas of the prairies which are not suited for the growing of coarse grains but are suited almost exclusively for the growing of wheat. Those people will continue to grow wheat, and the government has a responsibility to assist them in carrying that wheat by paying storage charges to them.
The sixth proposal was that the government should have a processing levy of 50 cents a bushel, the proceeds of that levy to be applied on the first 1,000 bushels delivered

Supply-State oj Agnculture
by each farmer. That would enable the government this year to pay 10 cents a bushel extra on the first 1,000 bushels-and again I have in mind the small farmer whose unit cost is high and who cannot hope to farm on the small acreage he will have this year at the rate of 70 cents basis Fort William.
These were the proposals that we made, but so far the government have given no reasons why they cannot accept them. The only statement we have had has been from the Minister of Agriculture who, as reported at page 1940 of Hansard, intimated that this policy would not be changed. He said that there might be changes in minor details, but that in the main, the policy would not be changed, that it was the government's considered policy, that it was the unanimous policy of the government.
When the minister says that it is the unanimous policy, I should like to know whose policy it is. It is not the wheat pools' policy if we are to judge by the statements of the western pools. It is not the united farmers' policy; certainly it has not been commended by the federation of agriculture. It certainly is not the policy of the Saskatchewan legislature or the two ministers who moved the resolution on February 28. This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture said, "No, it is the Canadian government's policy." But this Canadian government is a Liberal government, and there is a Liberal government in Saskatchewan. Surely the Liberal party has not one policy outside Saskatchewan and another one inside Saskatchewan. Surely it has not one policy in the place where it has no jurisdiction and another policy in this house, where it has jurisdiction. And yet that would appear to be the case. The minister says it is the unanimous policy of the government, but we cannot find any one in the house, apart from himself, who to date has spoken in favour of it, nor can we find any of the provincial governments bearing the Liberal label who have given to this policy their unqualified support.
We are therefore asking, since the government has not seen fit to accept any of the six proposals which I have outlined, that at least it shall consider accepting the six-point wheat policy proposed by the Saskatchewan legislature. We have never felt that it was adequate; we have felt in our group that there were one or two particulars in which it might be improved-for instance, the maximum delivery of 1,000 bushels. We have not felt that this was the most the government could be expected to do; we have felt that it was the very least the government could do.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Saskatchewan legislature goes much further than that. They ask for it all.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No. The Saskatchewan government asked that it be put on a quota basis. When I say 1,000 bushels from each farmer, I am not suggesting that all that should be accepted from each farmer is 1,000 bushels.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Saskatchewan government puts no limitation on the amount of wheat to be taken by the government.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The third suggestion of their resolution is "that the delivery of the 1941 crop be made on an acreage quota, such quota to be determined by storage space available during the crop year 1941." Therefore they recognize the necessity, as I think everyone does, of restricted delivery.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not say that.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. If you put it on an acreage quota basis you expect restricted delivery. When we speak of a maximum delivery of 1,000 bushels we are speaking of the maximum from each farmer on the first quarter, a lesser amount to be accepted from the other quarter-sections, according to storage space. But the idea is to allow the farmer, on the first quarter-section, to secure sufficient money to meet current obligations which will be pressing upon him next fall.
In order to give the house an opportunity to record its approval of the government's policy as compared with the proposals that have come from various agricultural organizations, summed up as they were in the resolution of the Saskatchewan legislature, I beg to move a subamendment, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson):
That the amendment be further amended byadding the following:
"And furthermore this house disapproves of the 1941 wheat marketing policy announced by the government on March 12, 1941, and urges as the minimum required in the present circumstances the consideration of the following six point wheat policy passed unanimously by the Saskatchewan legislature on February 28, 1941:
1.	That the minimum price for the 1941 wheat crop he set at 85 cents per bushel, basis No. 1 at Fort William;
2.	That a processing tax of 50 cents a bushel be levied on all wheat processed for consumption in Canada, the proceeds of such tax to be added to the minimum price of 85 cents a bushel.
3.	That the delivery of the 1941 crop be made on an acreage quota, such quota to be determined by the storage space available during the crop year 1941.
4.	That the government of Canada make advances to farmers for the purpose of providing funds with which to build essential farm storage.
Supply-State oj Agriculture

5.	That the government of Canada make provision for advances to farmers on the credit of the quota to be delivered.
6.	That the government of Canada maintain and carry the wheat surplus as an essential part of its war policy.
In moving that subamendment, we in this group have no desire to embarrass the government by a vote of no confidence, but we are anxious to give the members of this house what has been denied to them, an opportunity of expressing their approval or disapproval of a policy which has been brought into this house in a most surreptitious manner. We have tried to deal with this matter sympathetically. The hon. member for Moose Jaw said the other day that we were to be commended for the restraint and moderation of the proposals which we have made to the government. I doubt if any hon. member at this time wishes to make immoderate proposals to the government. We realize that the government is faced with a tremendous problem; we realize that it cannot accept at this time all the wheat grown; we realize that there must be restricted deliveries and that the farmers must be encouraged as much as possible to curtail wheat acreage. But at the same time we realize that to take $130,000,000 out of the pocket of the farmer and put back $30,000,000 compensation in the other pocket is to treat the farmer, as the minister has already said, in a manner in which no other people in Canada are being treated.
As far as we are concerned we are prepared to withdraw this motion if the government will accept the six-point wheat policy proposed by the Saskatchewan legislature as a basis for discussion with reference to the marketing of the 1941 wheat crop. Or we are prepared to withdraw it if the government will consider referring the whole question of a wheat policy for 1941 to a special committee of this house. As far as the $35,000,000 vote and the wheat acreage reduction bonus are concerned, that can go on; it is getting under way now. But all the regulations, the whole matter of the delivery and marketing of wheat are not pressing until some time in the latter part of July. Those regulations have not yet been brought down; that policy is still in a state of flux, and there is no reason why the whole government policy with reference to delivering wheat, the whole basis on which it will be accepted, whether or not there will be advances, how much the board will accept, should not be referred to a special committee; there is plenty of time. If the government is prepared to do that, we in our turn are prepared to withdraw this subamendment.

On the day the house adjourned for the Easter recess the Minister of Agriculture sought to give the impression, as reported on page 2278 of Hansard, that most of the recommendations made by agricultural organizations had been accepted, with the exception, he said, of the initial price. That is hardly correct. I wish to point out the things that are suggested in the six-point wheat policy and that are not to be found in the wheat policy announced by the government.

This afternoon the minister interrupted the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) to say with regard to the policy which he himself had enunciated on

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know whether the minister is a prophet or the son of a prophet, but I hope he is right. The strange thing is that the minister has so little confidence in his own prophecy that, while prophesying that at the end of five years we shall have removed all our wheat surplus-in fact I believe we are to be about 50,000,000 bushels short- he then proceeds to ask the farmers to reduce their wheat delivery this year to 48 per cent of what they delivered last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

The figures used in the statement were 380,000,000 bushels a year on an average. You have to grow

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Exactly; and has the minister any guarantee that by cutting down production to 230,000,000 bushels this year we will get that return plus the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are only cutting it down to 307,000,000 bushels this year.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, if you take into account the wheat necessary for seed. Has the minister any guarantee that during the next few years this country will grow sufficient wheat to make up for the reduction this year? Of course he has not. As a matter of fact, what this country is now proceeding to pay for is the result of a planless agriculture. The first time I listened to the Minister of Agriculture making a speech was in southern Saskatchewan in 1934. I remember that at that time he had a copy of a chart which was being circulated by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or the farmer-labour group as it was then known in Saskatchewan. I can still hear the minister warning the farmers in his audience of the dangers of regimentation and regaling them with a word picture of what would happen
2:522
Supply-State of Agriculture

if this new party ever got into power. I remember he had the audience howling with laughter when he told them they would have to telephone to Regina to see if they could put the south quarter in summer-fallow or if they would have to sow it in oats. That was very funny at that time, but unfortunately it has come true, not under the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation but under the party to which the minister belongs.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They still have to telephone to Regina.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If it were that easy, it would not be so bad.
I wish to conclude my remarks by saying that this afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a pointed comment. He said that nations are not defeated by an action this week or an action next week but are defeated by the disintegration of morale over a period of time. That is true. Every country that has been conquered by the nazi juggernaut has been conquered because the Germans have succeeded in creating mental confusion and defeatism among the population. I believe the British commonwealth of nations will win the war, but they will win it only if the morale of the people of these countries is of a higher type than the morale of the people of nazi Germany and fascist Italy. I believe hon. members will agree that the policy announced by the government has done more than anything of which I can think over many a year to undermine the morale of the people in the prairie provinces. No group of people in Canada have made more sacrifices or are more prepared to make sacrifices than the people who live between the great lakes and the Rocky mountains. But in this house on April 4 the minister himself frankly told them:
The farmers of western Canada know that this policy is not putting money into their pockets. . . . They know that this policy is taking money out of their pockets and making it possible for this dominion to finance the war to the extent of at least $100,000,000 more than would be the case if the government did for the wheat growers of the west what they are doing for most of the other people of Canada.
Then the minister went on the radio and made an appeal, pleading with the farmers for an additional sacrifice and telling them very frankly that they are being called upon to make greater sacrifices than any other group of people. In the face of all this, their feeling is only natural: Why should they be called upon to make greater sacrifices than anyone else? I do not need to remind this house that while agriculture has suffered by virtue of the war, and particularly those

branches of agriculture which depend upon the export market, other sections of this country have benefited by the war. I have no parish pump complex; I refuse to see Canada only through western eyes, but the fact does remain that this war has brought to the great industrial sections of Canada a measure of prosperity that they did not have before the war. We have pumped not millions but several hundred millions of dollars of war orders into the industrial areas, and in those areas they are enjoying a measure of prosperity they have not had for a good many years. It seems passing strange to the people of the prairie provinces that at this time they should be asked to make greater sacrifices than any other group of people in Canada, they who have less to give than any other group in this country.
We maintain that while the government cannot be expected to take unlimited quantities of wheat, as I said before; while they must make certain adaptations to meet an unusual crisis, they cannot escape two responsibilities. The first is to pay the farmer for the wheat he can deliver a price that will enable him to remain solvent. The second is to enable him to carry the wheat which the wheat board cannot accept, against that day when the people of Canada and the hungry people of the earth will be glad to get it.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to second this subamendment I feel that I am discussing one of the most important domestic problems to come before this parliament. I am sorry that in the discussion of agricultural matters some effort has been made to drive a wedge between eastern and western farmers. I can assure this house that those of us who are pleading for a better deal for western agriculture are quite familiar with the problems of farmers all across the dominion. Many of us left Ontario years ago after spending the early and perhaps the happier years of our lives on Ontario farms. We left Ontario because we felt that the future for agriculture here was not bright. That was the case at the end of the last century; that has been the case during each decade of the present century. We went west because the distant fields seemed green to us. During my lifetime at least, farmers, whether they lived in the maritimes, in central Canada, in the prairie provinces or in British Columbia, have never had a fair share of our national income. I resent very much the suggestion that has been made during this discussion on agriculture, that western people are asking for or have been receiving charity. It is our considered opinion

Supply-State of Agriculture
that the western plains have produced enormous quantities of new wealth in our Canadian economy; and if western farmers had received their fair share of that new wealth, they would not have found it necessary to appeal to federal governments in past years.
The province of Saskatchewan submitted to the Rowell-Sirois commission a brief which was prepared under the direction of Hon. T. C. Davis, now associate deputy minister of national war services. At page 225 of this brief two tables are presented to show what tariffs have cost western Canada, and what they have meant to eastern Canada. These tables were prepared in 1931 by the late Mr. Norman Rogers, and they indicate that only two provinces in Canada enjoyed a net per capita gain as a result of the tariff. Those two provinces showed a net gain, Quebec with one of SI 1.03 per person per year, and Ontario with 815.15. The other provinces showed net losses in the following amounts:

A careful study of these statistics indicates that directly or indirectly people living in Ontario have for a period of years enjoyed benefits derived from tariffs.
Another table I have before me appears in the report of the special committee set up in 1939 by the legislature of Saskatchewan to investigate farm implement prices. That committee presented a table showing where one's money goes when he buys a binder in Regina. A person who paid $167.02 for a binder in Regina in 1913 paid $45.56 for material, $11.97 for labour, $17.96 for overhead and 34 cents for experimental work, making a total cost of $75.83. The commission .amounted to $30.45, and the freight to $17.80. By 1926 those figures had increased to $77.50 for material, $28.85 for labour, $43.27 for overhead and 79 cents for experimental work, making a total cost of $150. The farmer paid $283 in Regina.
In 1936 a farmer paid $71.06 for the raw material in a binder, $22.62 for labour, $33.93 for overhead and $2.55 for experimental work, making a total cost of $130.16. Opposite that must be set the Regina price to the farmer of $281.
Hon. members will understand that during the time the farmers were compelled to pay such high prices for machinery they were not able to receive their fair share of what was 14873-147
produced. I would remind the house that western Canada was settled as part of a carefully considered national policy. Recently I read a statement made at the beginning of the century by one of the world's most famous scientists of that day, Sir William Crookes. He said:
The question of food supply is of urgent importance to-day and it is a life and death question for generations to come. England and all civilized nations stand in deadly peril of not having enough to eat.
Concluding he said:
Are we to go hungry, and to know the trial of scarcity? That is the poignant question. Thirty years is but a day in the life of a nation. Those present who may attend the meeting of the British Association thirty years hence will judge how far my forecasts are justified.
Thirty years have passed since Sir William made his forecast. Of course he was about as far astray as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was last November when he made his forecast in connection with the future of the wheat industry. Since Sir William made his prediction, new types of seed have been introduced. New types of labour-saving machinery have come to the market. Our western plains have been settled, and instead of a world shortage of food we have a world surplus.
Speaking recently, Vice-President Wallace said:
One hundred and fifty years ago it required nineteen people living on land to support themselves and one person in town. To-day, under greatly commercialized and industrialized conditions one person on the land supports himself and three persons in town, and contributes to the support of another person overseas. All this is a tribute to our technical genius as a people, and we may well be proud of it. Some day we will turn that genius to solve the problem of underconsumption. For the first time in history we are suffering because we have got too much of the things we need most. The science of production has outrun the science of distribution. We have got to catch our breath and catch up.
We have solved the problem of producing the world's supply of food, and we in western Canada have had no small part in the scheme of things. Some hon. members in the house have suggested that if western farmers had used good judgment, had they minded their own business and been thrifty, all their troubles would have been over. I have never been able to discover the culprit who has created that mythical individual in western Canada who has been pictured as going to California, British Columbia or Ontario after he has delivered the last bushel of wheat to the elevator, and spending the winter months in riotous living. I have lived a number of

speechtext:
In rising to
make my contribution to this debate and to give expression to the views of the people whom I have the honour to represent, I suggest in the first place that the amendment and the subamendment simply resolve themselves into motions of want of confidence in the government. As a farmer myself, I wish to go on record as declaring that agriculture,

Supply-State of Agriculture
so far as finances are concerned, is not in a healthy condition; but the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) proposes to the house that it be resolved that the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agriculture and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture, and in that regard I say that what he proposes has already been done in many of the various measures which have been taken since the Liberal government came into office. It began immediately after the putting into effect of the recent reciprocity agreement with the United States.
I know that farm prices are somewhat depressed, but we should face the facts. In the first place, I might comment upon the support which has been given to the amendments. When men of legal training show a special interest in agriculture, and when this is followed up by expressions from ministers of the gospel and everybody else on the other side except farmers, I begin to get rather suspicious of Greeks bearing gifts. When those who are not farmers show a special interest in agriculture, so much so that they are anxious to have a parity of prices, I am concerned about their sincerity.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order.
The hon. gentleman cannot question a member's sincerity.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Wait until I am through.
The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) moved a resolution which is a want of confidence, and by a certain coincidence, to fulfil the requirements of the rules of the house, that motion was withdrawn.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was to help the Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must admit that I am not
particularly familiar with the rules of the house; but I am prepared to say that the name of the hon. member for Haldimand is not on the present motion and it was convenient to him to withdraw it and he was glad to withdraw it. I suggest that at a time like this we should be putting our energies into the winning of the war instead of discussing politics.
The Conservative party has always taken a lofty attitude in its relations to Great Britain. It has always wrapped itself in the flag of loyalty and believed that it was the essence of everything that was good for British institutions. The members of that party would be making a patriotic gesture right now if the
[Mr. Wood.)
hon. member for Lake Centre would withdraw his motion and allow us to get on with the
business of the house.
Since, however, the motion is on the order paper and we are debating it, I wish to take the opportunity to make certain casual references to the condition of agriculture. We in Canada are suffering in consequence of a restriction of trade; there is no question about that; but I do say that the Canadian farmer to-day, in spite of these low prices, is enjoying the best agricultural prices of any agricultural country in the world except Great Britain. I defy any hon. member of the opposition to deny that. Take dairy products. Butter to-day is higher in Canada, in spite of the pegging of price, than in the United States. Up until just recently, bacon prices were about S3 higher in Canada than in the United States. These same men condemn the bacon board for allowing the importation of 24,000,000 pounds of bacon last year, but remember that the same law which allowed us to import that bacon has allowed us to export about 9,000 hogs so far this year. If we had taken the short view and cut off the importation of United States pork products last year and destroyed the reciprocity agreement, then we would not have that market to-day. By reason of the fact that prices of pork products were very low in the United States, there was a lowering of the production of hogs, and by virtue of that the price now has risen so that many Canadian hogs will go over to the United States market, proving that the policy of this government has been sound and that the parity of prices is being gradually adjusted.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the price of wheat?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I grant that wheat is the exception.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about eggs at eight cents a dozen at country points?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, anyone is foolish who sells eggs at eight cents a dozen.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Could the hon.
member give comparative prices of farm products in Canada and the United States?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot in all cases. I did
not expect to make this speech until to-morrow and the figures have not been forthcoming.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member said that agricultural prices in Canada are much higher than they are in the United

Supply-State of Agriculture
States, and I should like to know if he has the United States prices to compare with those in Canada?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Brant has the floor, and it is not permissible to interrupt him, except with his leave, in order to put a question.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did ask him a question.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And he cannot answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman has the floor.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have no objection to the hon. member asking a question, and I should like to supply him with the information, but to be frank, I did not expect to make this speech to-night. I shall have the figures forthcoming in due course. Comparing the condition of agriculture in Canada to-day with agriculture in the United States, I am prepared to say that agriculture in Canada is in a much healthier condition than in the United States, in spite of all the bonuses of the Roosevelt government for pig killing and all the unsound economic policies imposed upon agriculture there to advance it. And I would tell hon. members from the west, who seem to think the west is the only part of Canada that grows wheat or has any agricultural interest whatsoever, that bonusing of any kind is absolutely unsound. We cannot solve agricultural problems by sowing the taxpayers' money in summer-fallows or by bonusing pig-pens. I say that in spite of the fact that I raise a good many hogs myself on my own farm. That is not a solution of our problems.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What
about the cheese bonus?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The cheese bonus as far as this government is concerned is not a bonus; it is a premium for quality.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A distinction without a difference.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And a policy of encouragement of quality is quite within the bounds of proper development.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And how about Mr. Hepburn?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Hepburn enjoys the
distinction of having a large surplus due to the expansion of war industries financed by this government, $23,000,000 from corporation taxes. If he sees fit to hand some of that back to the farmers, I do not know that there
is any better place to put it because it immediately percolates into the whole of our economic life and every one gets a share. If he sees fit to do that, he is quite within his rights, but I say it is not going to solve the agricultural problem, if that is what the hon. leader of the opposition wishes me to say.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think we all agree with that.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I happen to be on the farm that my grandfather pioneered, and I do not believe that he ever got one cent of help from any government, or ever expected it.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But he was, I am sure, a good farmer.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was all right. I myself was born in the horse-and-buggy days, and when we sit down to three square meals a day we give thanks to the Almighty for it. I say that the solution of many of the farmers' problems is home-made. If hon. members try to debate the condition of agriculture from the point of view of dollars and cents, I might as well take my seat, because it cannot be done. Agriculture is the basis of our economic structure, but a farmer does not actually need as much money as others to be happy, because happiness is a home-made product.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But he needs money to pay his debts.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I quite understand that, but on the other hand there are many farmers who do not have debts; they wait for the money first. That side of the question ought to be considered as well.
This is a want of confidence motion, so I wish to draw the attention of the country and of this house to some of the accomplishments of this government. If the farmers' problems are to be solved, it cannot be done by taking money from the pocket of the general taxpayers. The farmers must assert themselves and solve their own problems. In 1939 we had a measure brought down called the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act, a measure to give financial assistance to any group of farmers who will associate themselves together to market their products, so that they have control of their own products and are in a position to demand a price commensurate with prices in other departments of our economic life. While I am a farmer myself, I could never understand why the farmer who in the past has consistently sold his brains and grey matter to other lines of industry, refuses to devote them to his own industry. If we had the brilliant men engaged in the marketing of agricultural products that we have furnished to the
Supply-State of Agriculture

ministry, the professions and the industrial life of this country, we would go a long way towards solving our problems. This measure could be a weapon in the hands of farmers, but so far they have not seized the opportunity provided by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in 1939 and proclaimed only about two months before the outbreak of the war. I commend that legislation to the attention of the Canadian federation of agriculture; instead of making speeches and condemning labour unions and industry for making so much money, let them sit round the table and use this grey matter to try to find a solution for their problems by cooperative effort.
I noticed that the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) was concerned about the high prices of agricultural implements. I am aware of the fact that there is a wide spread between what the farmer receives and what he has to pay for many articles, but I suggest to the hon. member for Mackenzie that we are still living in a free country. If we do not talk politics too long we may be able to keep it free; but if we lose too much time, it is hard to say what someone may tell the hon. member and myself to do. If the hon. gentleman thinks there is so much money to be made in manufacturing agricultural implements, why, does he not go into the business? I just happened to notice in the evening paper that Massey-Harris stock is quoted at $2.38, so he could buy one hundred shares for $238. He does not need to farm or do anything else; he can go into the business of making binders and mowers, and make these huge profits. That is my answer to his argument. You do not need to sit on a farm if you think there is more money to be made somewhere else.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The late president of Massey-Harris left an estate of nearly a million dollars, which is quite a lot more than is made by the farmer who runs the binder.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He had that before he went with Massey-Harris.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That might be because he was interested in a good many other matters.
I think it is a good thing to have some rich men in this country as long as they have the brains to go with their money, but it is a bad thing for men without brains to have a great deal of money.
Quite recently I saw in the Toronto Globe a statement by one of their scribes, Miss Macphail, which I believe requires a good deal of qualifying. It is a statement which also has been made in this house. Miss Macphail took the year 1937, which she said
(Mr. Wood.]
was the best year since the depression with the exception of the present year, and stated that in 1937 only nine per cent of the national income went to the farmers, who represent one-third of the population. I have heard that remark many times. Actually I do not think it is true. It may be that nine per cent of the national income came from agriculture; but when it is said that only nine per cent of the national income went to the farmers I do not believe it is true, because many farmers have incomes in addition to what they make from agriculture. The hon. member for Mackenzie suggested that the late president of the Massey-Harris company died a millionaire, but it does not necessarily follow that he made that money from the Massey-Harris company. Statements of this kind are made in an endeavour to get people to believe what somebody wants them to believe.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit a question, would he be good enough to define to this house what is national income, because that question has been bothering me for some months.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not an economist-

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Neither am I; that is my trouble.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -though I think I am perhaps as much of an economist as a good many of the people who say they are. Let me enlarge on that.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the national income of the farmers?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member or anyone else knows, because only about one per cent of the farmers keep books in order to know what their own income is.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You do not need to go to the farmers' books. All you need to do is to go to the bureau of statistics.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I respect and honour the bureau of statistics, but neither the bureau of statistics no.r anyone else knows how much I make on my farm.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They know what you get for what you sell, and that is your income.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I got some of it, anyway, and as long as I get the return from what I sell I am satisfied.
Then Miss Macphail went on to say that the average income of the Canadian farmer during the last ten years was about $473. That is just an estimate, but even if it is true,

Supply-State of Agriculture
I believe $473 is just about as good, living on the farm, as the average yearly earnings of people living in the city. That figure comes from the bureau of statistics; it may not be any more accurate than the other, but it is given as $956. Well, Mr. Speaker, if I am going to live in poverty I would rather live on a farm than in the city; and I think $473 on the farm is just as good as $956 in the city.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the gross income, is it not?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not interrupt the hon. member; and anyway, I cannot hear what he says.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that the gross income or the net income?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member will have to ask Miss Macphail.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I should like to remind hon. gentlemen that we are not in committee and that the rules do not allow the speaker to be interrupted, except with the speaker's leave, in order to put questions. The debate will become disorderly unless we adhere to that rule.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I appreciate your kindness in defending me, Mr. Speaker, but if I can make any contribution to the intelligence of hon. gentlemen in the far corner I am only too happy to do so. From what I have heard coming from that side I think they are badly in need of some enlightenment; and if I can help in any way I shall be glad to do so even if I do not follow the rules exactly.
With regard to agriculture I yield to no man in my desire to serve the farmer; but at the same time there are those who make statements that should not be made-and we have had an exhibition of it here to-night-who sometimes defeat the very purpose they set out to accomplish, though they may be sincere. I should like to refer to another statement by Miss Macphail:
The thing I'd like to see the farmer do in war time is go on strike, and I think something like that will have to come.
Much as I respect the author of this article, I wish to say that it is dangerous to make statements like that. I do not suppose Miss Macphail will welcome any guidance or direction from me, but I still have an opinion of my own, and I believe that in the agricultural districts we still have sober, sensible, straightthinking people who do not take kindly to assertions of this kind. Last December the president of the United Farmers' Cooperative, who is also secretary of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture-of which I am a member -made the statement that he would recommend that all farm boys leave the farms.
Of all the bad speeches that have been made in the Dominion of Canada I think that was the worst, because it created a great deal of dissension between farmers and their sons. I am inclined to take the view that some of these people who claim to be interested in the farmers are more anxious to make speeches, and that sometimes their tongues run a little ahead of their minds and they say things they really never intended to say.
My experience has been that the farmer whom I would want to guide and direct my business, the farmer from whom I would be prepared to take advice, is the man who is so busy minding his own business that he has no time to prepare speeches. That is the unfortunate thing. We as farmers should be in a position to obtain the services of some of these outstanding men. They may not be able to make very good speeches, but if you sit with them round a table you will get a sound philosophy of life which I am prepared to say I cannot get from men of any other profession or occupation. I believe that the solution of the problem of the farmers lies with the sober, straight-thinking farmer. I want to warn the federation of agriculture not to allow these other people to become too prominent by making statements of the kind I have mentioned, which is a form of fifth-column activity, a kind of sabotage as far as Canada is concerned. I do not hesitate to say that. I do not object to honest-to-goodness criticism; that is quite proper. But anything which lends itself bo upsetting the economic order, and undermining our institutions, does not lend itself to the best interests of national unity.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member infer there are hon. members in the house responsible for sabotage?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has named them.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does he sajr hon. members are a party to it?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have given certain quotations in which statements have been made. I do not wish to stipulate respecting every person in Canada, as to whether he or she did not make it. I say it was bad business to make those speeches. Hon. members in the house are at liberty to make their speeches. They have the protection of the house to say what they wish. But I would not want to be responsible for some of the statements which have been made by some hon. members.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon.
member will not be.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Another matter which in
the last few months has created considerable discussion has been the compulsory rail

Supply-State oj Agriculture

grading of hogs. That recommendation was made to the government by the bacon board, and as a result the government passed an order in council which became effective in October. I am prepared to admit that the rail grading of hogs takes away from the farmer the last opportunity he has for argument as to price. After the hog is on the rail, if the farmer is not satisfied as to grade he cannot load the hog into his wagon and take it home as he could if live grading had been carried out. I must say, however, the records show that rail grading has given the farmer a higher percentage of selects than live grading has given him. Furthermore, since it has been compulsory to rail-grade hog carcases in the six months of October, November, December, January, February and March, there has been an increase to the extent of five per cent in the number of grade A hogs. These figures show that there has been an improvement in hog grades, and that when the farmers have asserted themselves and marketed their hogs at the proper time, they have been successful in procuring an improvement in grading to the extent of five per cent since that regulation became effective.
In October, the percentage grading A stood at 28-5 for Ontario and 27 for Canada. In November, the percentage in Ontario stood at 29-3. It was 3T3 in December; and in January, 1941, it went up two points to 33-5. In February, it was 34-3, and in March, 34'7. These figures would prove that this measure, recommended by the government now in office, has had the effect of giving the farmer more money than he would have received had the measure not come into existence.
We must face the facts, whether we do or do not like rail grading. I like to see my hogs graded; but I realize that if we must cater to the market, and produce what is wanted by the consumer, then it is our duty to supply the trade with what it wants. We have evidence to show us that the policy of the government in this respect is sound. The farmer is to-day richer to a certain degree by reason of that policy than he was prior to the time it became effective.
If the subamendment, upon which we would first be asked to vote, were to be accepted, in this time of national crisis we would be calling upon the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation to form a government.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member wish to destroy us totally?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the original amendment were to carry, it would be incumbent upon the official opposition to form a government capable of carrying on. Regardless of what

happens, these motions are worded in an effort to make it impossible for hon. members to vote against them. I would point out, however, that we must take the long view. Is there any one in the opposition who is in a position to form a government? I would say that there is not, by any means.
For a few minutes let us view the record of the two parties in opposition responsible for these amendments. We have not a record of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in office, but we have a record of the official opposition. I do not wish to carry on a battle of recrimination, but it must be remembered that in these days we are at war. I believe that to-day the war effort of Canada is being carried on in a manner which commends itself to the serious-minded and sober-thinking citizens of the dominion.
Immediately upon the outbreak of the war, measures were passed taking care of excess profits. If there has been any opposition to the government, then I suggest it has come from those who have been unable to make a great deal of profit since we went to war. Prompt action was taken by the government right at the beginning of hostilities, and I have no doubt a great deal of criticism has been made because that action was taken. Surely, however, no man wants to wax wealthy from the blood of our young men who are called upon to defend this country, and to preserve our liberty. The government and the Prime Minister are to be commended for seeing to it that these measures were passed to safeguard the interests of our people. I believe that in the main the government's efforts have been successful.
There is no doubt that in administrations during this conflict there will be mistakes; that is only human. There will be instances when bad judgment may have been used. But in the main I believe that we have protected the people by many of the measures which have been passed. While some of those measures may not be popular, yet they have been instrumental in controlling inflation, that vicious thing which after the last war was responsible more than any other factor for bringing about the condition from which the agriculturist is suffering to-day.
The pegging of the price of butter was, I am prepared to admit, an unpopular move. In the long run, however, the farmer has not lost much by that action. At the time the peg was made, we were producing only
10,000,000 pounds of butter, and the trade was getting the other 20,000,000 pounds from the speculators. If the price of butter had continued to rise, it would have done no

Supply-State oj Agriculture
one any good, with the exception of the speculators. From now on, however, when the increase in production is so great, a few cents given immediately would do a great deal more for the wealth of the farmers than would have been the case, if given when he was producing only 10.000,000 pounds.
It was the lack of control in the last war which led to inflated prices. We had high prices at that time, and the result is that to-day some farmers are suffering because of the higher prices they paid for their farms than they should have paid. The inflation which took place at that time has been responsible for many of the disasters which have befallen agriculture. This government has taken steps to see that a similar state of affairs shall not exist. Efforts have been made to control prices of butter, wool, sugar, bread, leather and other commodities, so that they will not get out of control and command greater prices and ultimately reduce the purchasing power of the dollar of the Canadian citizen.
During the last conflict I sold hogs for $24 per hundred, but I had to take that same S24 and pay it out for a hundredweight of sugar. Therefore I was not anything ahead. I am inclined to the view that the parity of prices to-day is more favourable than that which existed during the last conflict. There was no control whatever at that time. If the amendment should happen to carry, will it mean that we shall have in power a government which will be of the same political complexion as that which was in power before and which permitted those things which were responsible for the disasters that occurred?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member should keep in mind the fact that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) belonged to the government of that day.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the minister was responsible for the horse deals, the drug scandals, and the amount of leather equipment which had to be abandoned-almost sixty per cent of the first year of the wrar effort of that government had to be scrapped-then he will have to take the responsibility. But he has since been converted, and it was not an eleventh hour conversion either. I believe there will be a seat for him in the high places. During a speech in Montreal before the national research council, the late General Sir Arthur Currie made a statement, which subsequent investigation proved to be right. He said that 150,000 more soldiers than were necessary had been sent overseas at a cost of $500,000,000. If fewer soldiers had been sent over with better equipment, perhaps we would not have had the large casualtv lists.
This country cannot afford to support the amendment or the subamendment. In the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) we have a man who will go down in history as an outstanding Canadian when the record of this conflict is written. I believe he will have the most exalted position of any Canadian statesman. His record will compare most favourably with that of Roosevelt and Churchill. The opposition has contended continuously that he has always leaned toward the United States. I am not sure that it should be called leaning; he was simply human and he wanted to have proper trade relations. But even though some people do call it leaning, it has proved to be one of the finest things, for he has reaped a rich harvest for the British empire. We had the reciprocity agreement of 1936 which was later renewed with the United Kingdom. There is nothing like trade to cement people together. Then we had the statement of the President of the United States at Ivy Lea that they would not stand idly by and see Canada invaded. Later on, we had the Ogdensburg agreement and the St. Lawrence waterway development, and just lately we have had the Hyde Park declaration. All these things must commend themselves to the people of Canada. Our leader has been termed a mild-mannered Prime Minister. He does not go out for headlines. Many men would make these arrangements the subject of great headlines, but he has done these things in his own quiet way.
There is nothing to commend the Conservative administration to the people of Canada. I do not believe you can name one act of social security which the Conservative administration ever provided for the Canadian people. Compare that record with the trade agreements, the old age pension legislation, the government annuity act and finally the unemployment insurance legislation.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Those were all Conservative acts.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It took a Liberal government to run the machinery.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What difference does it make; we are all Canadians.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then why should you be sponsoring a motion of want of confidence in the government? I can remember in 1911 when members of the Conservative party were talking so much about Laurier's tin-pot navy. Are they reallly proud of some of the speeches which were made at that time? In view of what has happened since, would it not have been better if Sir Wilfrid Laurier
Labour Conditions-Hamilton

had not been obstructed, if he had been permitted to develop a navy for Canada? In view of the attitude which our hon. friends have taken with regard to these policies, to move a vote of want of confidence in the splendid administration of the Prime Minister and his colleagues at this particular time when the country is struggling as never before, is a sorry spectacle to present to a self-respecting country.
On motion of Mr. Quelch the debate was adj oumed.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, April 29, 1941.
